A 4 by 4 table, part of the full all-pairs result, gives SimRank* scores for B, C, D, and E with 1 on the diagonal; the highlighted B, E cells read 0.30." width="100%"} SimRank* fixes the "zero-similarity problem" of the original SimRank, where most node pairs receive a score of 0.0 on real-world graphs, by considering asymmetric in-link paths. The result is a similarity matrix where each entry `s(a, b)` is in `[0, 1]`, with `s(a, a) = 1.0`. The idea behind SimRank-style measures is that two nodes are similar if they are linked from similar nodes. SimRank* follows paths of every length between the two nodes, with each extra step discounted by `importance_factor=`, so nodes that are close together or share neighbors score high and nodes in distant parts of the graph score low. The transition matrix is built from in-neighbors (edges pointing into each node); for undirected graphs, every neighbor counts. The raw solution is normalized so that every node has similarity `1.0` with itself and the matrix is symmetric. Use it for: - finding nodes that play similar roles or sit in similar neighborhoods (e.g., similar products in a co-purchase graph, related pages in a link graph) - building a similarity matrix for clustering, embedding, or recommendation - scoring pairs that share no direct neighbors, where `jaccard_coefficient()` and other local scores are all zero The computation works on a dense `n x n` matrix, so it needs *O(n²)* memory and *O(n³)* time; it is best suited to graphs with up to a few thousand nodes. Edge weights are ignored. To score a single pair, see `simrank_star_similarity_pair()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [importance_factor]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.8]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Decay factor `C`, which must be in `[0, 1)`. Each additional step along a path multiplies its contribution by roughly `C`, so higher values let similarity propagate further through the graph and raise off-diagonal scores, while lower values make scores depend mostly on immediate neighborhoods (and shrink toward `0`). Default is `0.8`. [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of fixed-point iterations for `method="iterative"`. Each iteration extends the paths considered by one step, so too few iterations underestimates (or misses) similarity between nodes that are only linked by longer paths. Ignored by `"closed_form"`. Default is `100`. [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-06]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence threshold for `method="iterative"`: iteration stops early once the overall (Frobenius-norm) change in the similarity matrix between two iterations falls below this value. Ignored by `"closed_form"`. Default is `1e-6`. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["closed_form"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Solver to use. `"closed_form"` (default) solves the PJsim Lyapunov equation exactly in *O(n³)* time via Bartels-Stewart (real Schur decomposition), so no iteration settings are needed. `"iterative"` uses fixed-point iteration in *O(K·n³)* time, where `K` is the number of iterations performed; it converges to the same values and is mainly useful for checking results or trading accuracy for an early stop. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return the raw nested dict `{node_a: {node_b: sim}}` without modifying the graph. If `False` (default), store each node's similarities as the node attribute `"simrank_star"` (overwriting any existing values), record the computation so it appears in `describe()`, and return the graph for chaining. Each node's value is a list of `{"node": other_id, "similarity": sim}` records sorted from most to least similar (ties by node ID), so it becomes a list-of-structs column in `get_node_df()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict, Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=True`, a nested dict mapping each node ID to a dict of `{other_node_id: similarity}`, including the node itself with `1.0`. Pairs whose similarity is zero are omitted from the inner dicts. Otherwise, the graph with a `"simrank_star"` node attribute holding each node's similarity records (zero pairs omitted here too). An empty graph yields an empty dict (or no attributes). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `importance_factor=` is outside `[0, 1)` or `method=` is not `"closed_form"` or `"iterative"`. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~simrank_star_similarity_pair`) : The score for a single pair. [](`~simrank_similarity`) : The original, which counts only walks of equal length. [](`~panther_similarity`) : Similarity from sharing sampled random paths. ## Examples {.doc-examples} SimRank* also counts paths that walkers take at different speeds, so a node is similar to its neighbors too. With `return_dict=True`, the scores come back as a nested dict: ::: {#04c78ef6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("B", "E")] ) label = graph.get_label_from_id scores = graph.simrank_star_similarity(return_dict=True)[ graph.get_id_from_label("A") ] dict(sorted((label(n), round(s, 3)) for n, s in scores.items())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 1.0, 'B': 0.403, 'C': 0.569, 'D': 0.569, 'E': 0.312} ``` ::: ::: ### Like Mara, by SimRank* `friends()` links 24 members of two clubs in a made-up town, a chess club and a climbing club, who are friends. SimRank ranks Pablo, with the same friends, first among those like Mara. SimRank* counts paths of any shape between them, so her three friends now rank ahead of Pablo: ::: {#f4065ab1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = ec.friends() label = friends.get_label_from_id mara = friends.simrank_star_similarity(return_dict=True)[ friends.get_id_from_label("Mara") ] others = { label(n): round(s, 2) for n, s in mara.items() if label(n) != "Mara" } sorted(others.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1])[:5] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('Nico', 0.44), ('Rosa', 0.39), ('Oona', 0.37), ('Pablo', 0.32), ('Sven', 0.14)] ``` ::: ::: Without `return_dict=True`, each person's scores are stored as a `simrank_star` node attribute, most similar first: ::: {#d21ee7e1 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} friends = friends.simrank_star_similarity() friends.get_node_df().select("label", "simrank_star").head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
